Boundedness and finite-time blow-up in a quasilinear parabolic–elliptic chemotaxis system
with logistic source and nonlinear production

Yuya Tanaka00 0 E-mail: yuya.tns.6308@gmail.com

Department of Mathematics, Tokyo University of Science

1-3, Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan

August 24, 2026

  • Abstract. This paper deals with the quasilinear parabolic–elliptic chemotaxis system with logistic source and nonlinear production,

    {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(S(u)∇v)+λu−μuκ,x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−Mf¯​(t)+f⁡(u),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(S(u)\nabla v)+\lambda u-\mu u^{\kappa},&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ 0=\Delta v-\overline{M_{f}}(t)+f(u),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{cases}

    where λ>0\lambda>0, μ>0\mu>0, κ>1\kappa>1 and Mf¯​(t):=1|Ω|​∫Ωf⁡(u⁡(x,t))​𝑑x\overline{M_{f}}(t):=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}f(u(x,t))\,dx, and DD, SS and ff are functions generalizing the prototypes

    D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1,S⁡(u)=u​(u+1)α−1​and​f​(u)=uℓ\displaystyle D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1},\hskip 8.50012ptS(u)=u(u+1)^{\alpha-1}\hskip 8.50012pt\mbox{and}\hskip 8.50012ptf(u)=u^{\ell}

    with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R}, α>0\alpha>0 and ℓ>0\ell>0. In the case m=α=ℓ=1m=\alpha=\ell=1, Fuest (NoDEA Nonlinear Differential Equations Appl.; 2021; 28; 16) obtained conditions for κ\kappa such that solutions blow up in finite time. However, in the above system boundedness and finite-time blow-up of solutions have been not yet established. This paper gives boundedness and finite-time blow-up under some conditions for mm, α\alpha, κ\kappa and ℓ\ell.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the following quasilinear parabolic–elliptic chemotaxis system with logistic source and nonlinear production:

(1.1) {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(S(u)∇v)+λu−μuκ,x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−Mf¯​(t)+f⁡(u),x∈Ω,t>0,∇u⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(S(u)\nabla v)+\lambda u-\mu u^{\kappa},&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ 0=\Delta v-\overline{M_{f}}(t)+f(u),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \nabla u\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases}

where Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\ (n\geq 1) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega; λ>0\lambda>0, μ>0\mu>0 and κ>1\kappa>1; D,S∈C2​([0,∞))D,S\in C^{2}([0,\infty)) and D⁡(0)>0D(0)>0; f∈⋃β∈(0,1)Clocβ​([0,∞))∩C1​((0,∞))f\in\bigcup_{\beta\in(0,1)}C_{\rm loc}^{\beta}([0,\infty))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty));

Mf¯​(t):=1|Ω|​∫Ωf⁡(u⁡(x,t))​𝑑x;\overline{M_{f}}(t):=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}f(u(x,t))\,dx;

ν\nu is the outward normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega; u0∈⋃β∈(0,1)Cβ​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in\bigcup_{\beta\in(0,1)}C^{\beta}(\overline{\Omega}) is nonnegative.

The system (1.1) describes a motion of cellular slime molds with chemotaxis, and the unknown function u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) donates the density of cells and the unknown function v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) represents the concentration of the chemical substance at place x∈Ωx\in\Omega and time t>0t>0. This system is one of many types of the Keller–Segel system

(1.2) {ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{cases}

which was proposed by Keller and Segel [9]. A number of variations of the original system (1.2) and related results for blow-up (in the radial setting) and boundedness are introduced in [1, 6, 11]:

  • •

    We first focus on the quasilinear Keller–Segel system,

    {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(S(u)∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+f⁡(u),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(S(u)\nabla v),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+f(u),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{cases}

    where τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. When f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u, in the parabolic–parabolic setting (τ=1)(\tau=1), Tao and Winkler [17] showed that solutions are global and bounded under the conditions that S⁡(u)D⁡(u)≤c​uq\frac{S(u)}{D(u)}\leq cu^{q} with q<2nq<\frac{2}{n} and c>0c>0 and that Ω\Omega is a convex domain; Ishida et al. [7] removed the convexity of Ω\Omega; whereas Winkler [21] proved that solutions blow up in either finite or infinite time when S⁡(u)D⁡(u)≥c​uq\frac{S(u)}{D(u)}\geq cu^{q} with q>2nq>\frac{2}{n} and c>0c>0; In the parabolic–elliptic setting (τ=0)(\tau=0), Lankeit [10] proved that solutions exist globally and are bounded in the case q<2nq<\frac{2}{n} and that unbounded solutions are constructed in the case q>2nq>\frac{2}{n}. When τ=1\tau=1 and D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1, S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u and f⁡(u)=uℓf(u)=u^{\ell} with ℓ>0\ell>0, Liu and Tao [13] established global existence and boundedness under the condition that 0<ℓ<2n0<\ell<\frac{2}{n}; Moreover, in the case that D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} and S⁡(u)=u​(1+u)α−1S(u)=u(1+u)^{\alpha-1} with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R} and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, it was obtained that solutions are global and bounded under the condition α−m+max⁡{ℓ,1n}<2n\alpha-m+\max\left\{\ell,\frac{1}{n}\right\}<\frac{2}{n} in [15].

  • •

    We next review the quasilinear Keller–Segel system with logistic source,

    {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(S(u)∇v)+λu−μuκ,x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−v+f⁡(u),x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(S(u)\nabla v)+\lambda u-\mu u^{\kappa},&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+f(u),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\end{cases}

    where λ>0\lambda>0, μ>0\mu>0, κ>1\kappa>1 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. As to this system, blow-up phenomena are suppressed when κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 and f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u. Indeed, in the parabolic–parabolic setting (τ=1\tau=1), when D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1 and S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u, Winkler [20] derived that solutions exist globally and are bounded if μ>0\mu>0 is so large and κ=2\kappa=2; When D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} and S⁡(u)=u​(u+1)α−1S(u)=u(u+1)^{\alpha-1} with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R} and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, global existence and boundedness were obtained if λ=μ=1\lambda=\mu=1, κ=2\kappa=2 and 0<α−m+1<44+n0<\alpha-m+1<\frac{4}{4+n} by Zheng [28]. In the parabolic–elliptic setting (τ=0)(\tau=0), when D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1 and S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u, Tello and Winker [18] showed that solutions exist globally and are bounded in the cases that κ=2\kappa=2 and μ>max⁡{0,n−2n}\mu>\max\left\{0,\frac{n-2}{n}\right\} and that κ>2\kappa>2 and μ>0\mu>0; When D⁡(u)=um−1D(u)=u^{m-1} and S⁡(u)=uαS(u)=u^{\alpha} for all u≥1u\geq 1 with m≥1m\geq 1 and α>0\alpha>0, Zheng [27] proved global existence and boundedness in the cases that κ>1\kappa>1 and α+1<max⁡{m+2n,κ}\alpha+1<\max\left\{m+\frac{2}{n},\kappa\right\} and that κ>1\kappa>1, α+1=κ\alpha+1=\kappa and μ>μ0\mu>\mu_{0} for some μ0>0\mu_{0}>0. On the other hands, in the parabolic–elliptic setting, it is known that blow-up occurs under the some conditions for κ>1\kappa>1 when f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u. When D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1 and S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u, Winkler [24] presented that if 1<κ<76​(n∈{3,4})1<\kappa<\frac{7}{6}\ (n\in\{3,4\}) and 1<κ<1+12​(n−1)​(n≥5)1<\kappa<1+\frac{1}{2(n-1)}\ (n\geq 5), then solutions blow up in finite time; Similar blow-up results were obtained in the case that D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} and S⁡(u)=u​(u+1)α−1S(u)=u(u+1)^{\alpha-1} with m≥1m\geq 1 and α>0\alpha>0 (see [2, 14, 16]).

    We turn our eyes into the quasilinear parabolic–elliptic chemotaxis system

    {ut=∇⋅(D(u)∇u)−∇⋅(S(u)∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,0=Δ​v−Mf¯​(t)+f⁡(u),x∈Ω,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(D(u)\nabla u)-\nabla\cdot(S(u)\nabla v),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ 0=\Delta v-\overline{M_{f}}(t)+f(u),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0.\end{cases}

    A simplification of this system was introduced by Jöger and Luckhaus [8]. When D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R}, S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u and f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u, Cieślak and Winkler [3] derived global existence and boundedness in the case 2−m<2n2-m<\frac{2}{n} and finite-time blow-up in the case 2−m>2n2-m>\frac{2}{n}; When D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} and S⁡(u)=u​(u+1)α−1S(u)=u(u+1)^{\alpha-1} with m≤1m\leq 1 and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} as well as f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u, Winkler and Djie [25] proved that solutions are global and bounded if α−m+1<2n\alpha-m+1<\frac{2}{n}, whereas finite-time blow-up occurs if α−m+1>2n\alpha-m+1>\frac{2}{n}; When D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1, S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u and f⁡(u)=uℓf(u)=u^{\ell} with ℓ>0\ell>0, Winkler [23] obtained that solutions exist globally and remain bounded in the case ℓ<2n\ell<\frac{2}{n} and that there exist solutions which are unbounded in finite time in the case ℓ>2n\ell>\frac{2}{n}; When D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1}, S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u and f⁡(u)=uℓf(u)=u^{\ell} with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R} and ℓ>0\ell>0, global existence and boundedness were established if ℓ−m+1<2n\ell-m+1<\frac{2}{n} by Li [12]. Moreover, in [12] it was asserted that finite-time blow-up occurs under the condition that ℓ−m+1>2n\ell-m+1>\frac{2}{n}. However, this condition should be repaired because from assumptions of [12, Lemma 3.5] we can obtain the condition that

    (1.3) ℓ−(m−1)+>2n,where(m−1)+:=max⁡{0,m−1};\ell-(m-1)_{+}>\frac{2}{n},\quad\mbox{where}\quad(m-1)_{+}:=\max\{0,m-1\};

    When D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1, S⁡(u)=u​(u+1)α−1S(u)=u(u+1)^{\alpha-1} and f⁡(u)=uℓf(u)=u^{\ell} with α>0\alpha>0 and ℓ>0\ell>0, Wang and Li [19] derived the critical value α+ℓ−1=2n\alpha+\ell-1=\frac{2}{n}.

  • •

    In the system (1.1), when D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1, S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u and f⁡(u)=uf(u)=u, Winkler [22] showed that if 1<κ<32+12​n−2​(n≥5)1<\kappa<\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2n-2}\ (n\geq 5), then there exists a solution blowing up in finite time; Moreover, a similar blow-up result was obtained in the case that D⁡(u)=(u+1)m−1D(u)=(u+1)^{m-1} with m≥1m\geq 1 in [2]; Furthermore, Fuest [5] showed that solutions blow up in finite time under the conditions that 1<κ<min⁡{2,n2}1<\kappa<\min\left\{2,\frac{n}{2}\right\} and μ>0​(n≥3)\mu>0\ (n\geq 3) and that κ=2\kappa=2 and μ∈(0,n−4n)​(n≥5)\mu\in\left(0,\frac{n-4}{n}\right)\ (n\geq 5); In the two dimensional setting and κ=2\kappa=2, global existence and boundedness were established when ∫Ωu0<8​π\int_{\Omega}u_{0}<8\pi, whereas finite-time blow-up occurs when ∫Ωu0<m0\int_{\Omega}u_{0}<m_{0} with m0>8​πm_{0}>8\pi in [4].

In summary, in [2, 4, 5, 22], blow-up results were derived in the chemotaxis system with logistic source and linear production. However, boundedness and blow-up results were not obtained in the quasilinear chemotaxis system with logistic source and nonlinear production (when D⁡(u)=1D(u)=1 and S⁡(u)=uS(u)=u, recently, Yi et al. [26] derived the blow-up result under the condition that ℓ+1>κ⁡(1+2n)\ell+1>\kappa\left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right)).

Our aim of this paper is to present conditions that solutions of (1.1) are bounded or blow up. Before we state the main results, we give conditions for the functions DD, SS and ff as follows:

(1.4) D\displaystyle D ∈C2​([0,∞))​is positive;\displaystyle\in C^{2}([0,\infty))\ \mbox{is positive};
(1.5) S\displaystyle S ∈C2​([0,∞))​is nonnegative and nondecreasing;\displaystyle\in C^{2}([0,\infty))\ \mbox{is nonnegative and nondecreasing};
(1.6) f\displaystyle f ∈⋃β∈(0,1)Clocβ​([0,∞))∩C1​((0,∞))​is nonnegative and nondecreasing.\displaystyle\in\bigcup_{\beta\in(0,1)}C_{\rm loc}^{\beta}([0,\infty))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty))\ \mbox{is nonnegative and nondecreasing}.

We now state the main theorems. The first one asserts boundedness of solutions.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\ (n\geq 1) be a smooth bounded domain, and let δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1], m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R}, α>0\alpha>0, λ>0\lambda>0, μ>0\mu>0, κ>1\kappa>1 and ℓ>0\ell>0. Assume that u0∈⋃β∈(0,1)Cβ​(Ω¯)u_{0}\in\bigcup_{\beta\in(0,1)}C^{\beta}(\overline{\Omega}) is nonnegative and DD, SS and ff satisfy (1.4), (1.5) and (1.6) as well as

(1.7) D⁡(ξ)≥CD​(ξ+δ)m−1,S⁡(ξ)≤CS​ξ​(ξ+δ)α−1for all​ξ≥0\displaystyle D(\xi)\geq C_{D}(\xi+\delta)^{m-1},\quad S(\xi)\leq C_{S}\xi(\xi+\delta)^{\alpha-1}\quad\mbox{for all}\ \xi\geq 0

and

(1.8) f⁡(ξ)≤L​ξℓfor all​ξ≥0\displaystyle f(\xi)\leq L\xi^{\ell}\quad\mbox{for all}\ \xi\geq 0

with CD>0C_{D}>0, CS>0C_{S}>0 and L>0L>0. Suppose that mm, α\alpha, μ\mu, κ\kappa and ℓ\ell fulfill that

(1.9) if​α+ℓ\displaystyle\mbox{if}\ \alpha+\ell <max⁡{m+2n,κ},\displaystyle<\max\left\{m+\frac{2}{n},\kappa\right\}, thenμ>0,\displaystyle\quad\mbox{then}\quad\mu>0,
(1.10) if​α+ℓ\displaystyle\mbox{if}\ \alpha+\ell =κ,\displaystyle=\kappa, thenμ>n⁡(α+ℓ−m)−22​(α−1)+n⁡(α+ℓ−m)​CS​L.\displaystyle\quad\mbox{then}\quad\mu>\frac{n(\alpha+\ell-m)-2}{2(\alpha-1)+n(\alpha+\ell-m)}C_{S}L.

Then there exists an exactly one pair (u,v)(u,v) of functions

{u∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞)),v∈⋂q>nC0​([0,∞),W1,q​(Ω))∩C2,0​(Ω¯×(0,∞))\displaystyle\begin{cases}u\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty)),\\ v\in\bigcap_{q>n}C^{0}([0,\infty);W^{1,q}(\Omega))\cap C^{2,0}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))\end{cases}

which solves (1.1) classically. Moreover, the solution (u,v)(u,v) is bounded in the sense that there exists C>0C>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤Cfor all​t∈(0,∞).\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(0,\infty).

We next state a result such that solutions blow up in finite time.

Remark 1.1.

As to Theorem 1.1, letting κ→1\kappa\to 1 implies that the condition (1.9) reduces the condition

α+ℓ<max⁡{m+2n,1},\alpha+\ell<\max\left\{m+\frac{2}{n},1\right\},

which is a generalized condition such that solutions remain bounded in [12, 19, 23]. Also, as to Theorem 1.2, we see that the condition (1.13) with m=1m=1 and κ→1\kappa\to 1 is a generalized condition such that solutions blow up in finite time in [19, 23].

Remark 1.2.

When α=1\alpha=1, letting κ→1\kappa\to 1 entails from (1.13) and (1.14) that

(1.17) if​m≥0,thenℓ>max⁡{m−1+2n,0},\displaystyle\mbox{if}\ m\geq 0,\quad\mbox{then}\quad\ell>\max\left\{m-1+\frac{2}{n},0\right\},
(1.18) if​m<0,thenℓ>max⁡{−1+2n,0}.\displaystyle\mbox{if}\ m<0,\quad\mbox{then}\quad\ell>\max\left\{-1+\frac{2}{n},0\right\}.

For instance, when m≤1−2nm\leq 1-\frac{2}{n}, we obtain from (1.3) that ℓ>2n\ell>\frac{2}{n}, whereas we can observe from (1.17) and (1.18) that ℓ>{2n−1,0}\ell>\left\{\frac{2}{n}-1,0\right\}. Thus the conditions (1.17) and (1.18) improve the condition in [12].

Moreover, in the case that m=1m=1 and α=1\alpha=1, we can establish that

(1.19) 1+ℓ>max⁡{1+2n​κ,κ}.\displaystyle 1+\ell>\max\left\{1+\frac{2}{n}\kappa,\kappa\right\}.

Because (1+2n)​κ>max⁡{1+2n​κ,κ}\left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right)\kappa>\max\left\{1+\frac{2}{n}\kappa,\kappa\right\}, we can make sure that the condition (1.19) is an improvement on the condition in [26].

The proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 are based on those in [23]. As to the proof of Theorem 1.1, our purpose is to establish an LpL^{p}-estimate for uu. In order to obtain an LpL^{p}-estimate, we consider three cases. With regard to the proof of Theorem 1.2, we first define the mass accumulation function

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall local existence and show Theorem 1.1. In Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.2 and give open problems.

2 Boundedness

In this section we derive global existence and boundedness in (1.1). We first introduce a result on local existence of classical solutions to (1.1). This lemma can be proved by a standard fixed point argument (see e.g., [25]).

2.4 Proof of Theorem 1.1

In this subsection we complete the proof of boundedness.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Thanks to (1.9) and (1.10), we can apply Lemmas 2.3, 2.4 and 2.6. Therefore, for any p>1p>1 we can find c1>0c_{1}>0 such that

∫Ωup​𝑑x≤c1\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\,dx\leq c_{1}

for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\rm max}). By the Moser iteration (see [17, Lemma A.1]), we obtain

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤∞\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\infty

for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\rm max}), which concludes the proof. ∎

3.4 Open problems

In [5, 19, 23] the critical values such that solutions remain bounded or blow up in finite time were derived. With regard to the conditions (1.9), (1.13) and (1.14), we see that if n≥3n\geq 3 and m≥0m\geq 0 as well as nn−2​m≤κ\frac{n}{n-2}m\leq\kappa, then

max⁡{m+2n,κ}=max⁡{m+2n​κ,κ}=κ.\max\left\{m+\frac{2}{n},\kappa\right\}=\max\left\{m+\frac{2}{n}\kappa,\kappa\right\}=\kappa.

Thus we know that the critical value is α+ℓ=κ\alpha+\ell=\kappa in this case. However, in the cases that n∈{1,2}n\in\{1,2\} and that n≥3n\geq 3 and m≥0m\geq 0 as well as nn−2​m>κ\frac{n}{n-2}m>\kappa, the conditions (1.9), (1.13) and (1.14) are not optimal. Moreover, the special cases are as follows:

  • •

    In the case that m=α=1m=\alpha=1, behavior of solutions is an open problem when max⁡{2n,κ−1}≤ℓ≤2n​κ\max\left\{\frac{2}{n},\kappa-1\right\}\leq\ell\leq\frac{2}{n}\kappa (see Figures 6 and 6).

  • •

    In the case that m=1m=1 and κ<n(n−2)+\kappa<\frac{n}{(n-2)_{+}}, from Figure 7 we have an open question of whether solutions remain bounded or blow up when max⁡{1+2n,κ}≤α+ℓ≤1+2n​κ\max\left\{1+\frac{2}{n},\kappa\right\}\leq\alpha+\ell\leq 1+\frac{2}{n}\kappa.

  • •

    In the case that α=1\alpha=1 and ℓ>0\ell>0, there is an open problem for behavior of solutions when n=1n=1 and max⁡{κ−1,m+1}≤ℓ≤max⁡{2​κ−1,m+2​κ−1}\max\{\kappa-1,m+1\}\leq\ell\leq\max\{2\kappa-1,m+2\kappa-1\}. Also, the same question exists when n≥2n\geq 2 and max⁡{κ−1,m−(1−2n)}≤ℓ≤m−(1−2n​κ)\max\left\{\kappa-1,m-\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\right)\right\}\leq\ell\leq m-\left(1-\frac{2}{n}\kappa\right). Moreover, in the case that α>0\alpha>0 and ℓ=1\ell=1, we obtain regions that ℓ\ell is replaced by α\alpha in Figures 9 and 9.
